title: Wildfire Response: Are We Prepared for the New Normal?
label: 15 Sep 2026 · Wildfire preparedness
summary: This hearing examined the UK Government's response to the unprecedented 2026 wildfire season, which saw record numbers of fires, homes destroyed and over 50,000 acres burned. Two new ministers from DEFRA and MHCLG, along with senior officials, faced questions on lessons learned, the adequacy of resources, the national risk register, emergency alerts, land management and planning. The session revealed cross-government efforts but also gaps in strategy, coordination with devolved administrations, and urgency ahead of the next fire season. The main conclusion was that the current approach is not fit for future risk and that a step change in prevention, preparedness and resourcing is needed.

chapters.title: Lessons from a Record Wildfire Season
chapters.takeaway: The 2026 wildfire season was unprecedented and showed that current systems are not fit for the future; both departments acknowledge the need for a major rethink.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This summer was dreadful for wildfires: record numbers, 19 homes destroyed, over 50,000 acres burned. Ministers, what lessons have you drawn?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We're in a very different place now. We had over 1,300 wildfires—record numbers. What we have in place now won't be fit for managing fires in 10 years. We need to look again at land management, responsiveness, and behaviour change.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I agree. The summer showed incredible professionalism from fire services, but also that we now face urban fringe fires threatening homes and infrastructure. It's about prevention, mitigation, recovery, and response. Future preparedness is critical.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: People in rural areas have lived with this for years. It took homes burning in Stourbridge for the Prime Minister to convene Cobra and appoint a fire minister. Is that what it takes?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The scale brought wider public understanding. I've seen the devastation locally. The Prime Minister is committed to a wildfire summit in October, bringing together all involved, including community representatives.

chapters.title: Coordination and Resources
chapters.takeaway: There is cross-government work but no dedicated national wildfire strategy yet; resources may need to be reallocated, and coordination with devolved administrations needs ministerial engagement.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Baroness Blake, this summer exposed major gaps. The Staffordshire Chief Fire Officer said they were stretched and lacked appliance availability. Do you accept that?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Absolutely. The changing pattern means we must look at how we allocate resources. We have pilots on equipment and are learning from this summer. We put £97 million into resilience before the summer.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: We have no national wildfire strategy in England. Will you commit to publishing one before next season?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: I'm focused on a one-year, two-year, and 10-year vision. We're increasing resources in DEFRA. We're working on an action plan that will feed into the summit. The strategy will be iterative.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We're not waiting for a strategy to coordinate. We have joint governance between our departments, but coordination across government hasn't been good enough. This is a catalyst.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Have you spoken to your counterparts in Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I haven't yet, but officials are in regular contact. We need better political coordination.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We engage regularly with devolved administrations. We were in Scotland three weeks ago. There's no rebuff; we work closely.

chapters.title: Aerial Firefighting and Technology
chapters.takeaway: The UK lacks dedicated aerial firefighting assets and relies on commercial arrangements; the government is exploring cost-effective solutions including drones and military assets.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The UK doesn't have a dedicated aerial firefighting capability. Relying on local commercial providers isn't sufficient, is it?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Aerial support is top of the agenda for the summit. Fire chiefs say it's good at putting out flames but not the underlying fire. We're looking at options.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We've relied on fire services resourcing themselves, but 44 services competing for the same asset isn't cost-effective. We're talking to providers about on-call availability for next summer. We're also looking at drones. We need to solve this for next summer and the future.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about using military assets, like Chinooks?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: The RAF is in discussions. We're looking at all public and private sector assets. Nothing is off the table.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Do you have a timeline?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: By next summer we need to be in a much better place. That's what we're holding ourselves accountable for.

chapters.title: Land Management and Controlled Burning
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA is reviewing licensing for controlled burning but maintains that long-term peatland restoration is the goal; critics argue the licensing scheme is too restrictive and slow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On fuel load: re-wetting takes decades. What are you doing to reduce fire load for next year?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Cutting is an option where accessible. We've granted two licences where cutting wasn't possible. Peatland restoration is a long-term solution.

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: The licensing scheme applies to deep peat. We've had 24 applications; most were for training, which the fire service says can be done elsewhere. We're working with the CLA to make the process more flexible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Even though land managers say they need seasonal burning, they're not applying because the regulations are too restrictive.

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: We're in live conversations to improve guidance before the next burning season. It's not a blanket ban; we'll issue licences for credible wildfire mitigation.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The evidence review didn't consider wildfire risk. Does that concern you?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: We take advice from fire services on each application. We also consider wildfire risk in policy decisions. Evidence is never perfect, but we refine it.

chapters.title: Emergency Alerts and Risk Assessment
chapters.takeaway: The national emergency alert was issued on fire service advice but faced technical and language issues; the national risk register underestimates wildfire likelihood and will be updated.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The emergency alert on 14 August was a significant moment. Should it have been issued sooner?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: There are different views. On balance, it was beneficial, but we need sophisticated procedures. Vulnerable people and language sequencing in Wales were issues. We must use it judiciously.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The decision was taken on the advice of the fire service. It raised public awareness but there were technical issues like repeated alerts due to poor signal. We're learning from that.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The national risk register rates wildfire as remote—less likely than a volcanic eruption. Is that accurate?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The evidence shows realities have shifted. We're preparing for increased risk due to climate change.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We knew risk was changing but the speed was significant. We had 11 major incidents on one day. The risk register needs updating, and we'll do that before next season.

chapters.title: Planning, Water and Local Powers
chapters.takeaway: Wildfire risk is being incorporated into planning policy, but water availability and local powers to restrict dangerous activities like disposable barbecues need further work.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What role did fire services have in shaping the 2026 planning framework's wildfire risk provisions?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: I wasn't directly involved, but I believe they were consulted via the National Fire Chiefs Council. Simple measures like fire breaks can slow fire spread and give fire services time.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Wildfire risk must be part of the overall planning package, not stand-alone. We're considering guidance on managing risk in new developments.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Water availability is a growing challenge. Should water companies have stronger requirements to support firefighting?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I don't have an answer yet, but we're gathering evidence. Water companies are represented on local resilience forums and fire services work with them operationally.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We need water resilience. Water companies must invest in infrastructure. We have a drought working group with water companies and the EA.

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: Water companies have a legal duty for emergency preparedness. We'll take away the specific point about pressure during fires.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should land managers be able to create wildfire ponds through permitted development rights?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We're working with the NFU on permitted development rights for on-farm reservoirs. Wildfire ponds will be given full consideration.

chapters.title: Joint Response and Future Preparedness
chapters.takeaway: The government is strengthening partnerships and adaptation plans, but faces budget constraints and needs to urgently improve preparedness before the next wildfire season.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What steps are you taking to strengthen partnerships between fire services, land managers, and communities?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We're focusing on a one-year, two-year, and 10-year vision. Land managers must work with fire services to reassess land. We need more uptake of land management schemes for fire resilience.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Local resilience forums are key. They need to be bespoke to local challenges and share intelligence. We must support the health and wellbeing of firefighters too.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Climate Change Committee says national adaptation plan 3 is not fit for purpose. Will plan 4 be radically different?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We'll set stronger objectives in adaptation 4, preparing for at least 2°C warming by 2050. But we're not waiting—actions are happening now, like the wildfire summit.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Will you have the budget you need?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We need to be evidence-led. There's money in ELM schemes not being taken up. We'll focus on behaviour change and technology. Funding will follow a planned, evidence-based response.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We've run over, but I'll leave you with this: instil a sense of urgency. September now; next fire season will be here before we know it. It's your job to make sure the machinery of government doesn't grind slowly.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I take that point. We're looking carefully at the health and wellbeing of firefighters—they keep us safe. That's alongside all the other work.
